title: Thomas Sunday
hookLine: the Sunday after Easter remembers Thomas; Catholics also keep Divine Mercy Sunday

lines: HE WAS OUT WHEN IT HAPPENED.
cards: Thomas was out when it happened. His friends find him and tell him they've seen Jesus alive, and he answers them plainly.

In the King James Bible: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." He isn't rude about it.
He just says what it would take. Nothing secondhand. For eight days the story leaves him there, the one in the room who can't say what everyone else is saying.
In the Orthodox calendar, the Sunday after Easter is named for him. Today, Thomas Sunday.

teach.b: John tells it: "after eight days again his disciples were within, and Thomas with them." Doors shut. Jesus stands among them and says, "Peace be unto you."

Then he turns to Thomas and offers exactly what he asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." Notice two things.
Jesus doesn't refuse the request; he answers it almost word for word. And John never says Thomas actually touched him.
Some paintings show his finger in the wound, but the text goes straight to what he says: "My Lord and my God." The one who doubted out loud is the one who says it, face to face.
Then a line for everyone who wasn't in that room: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." Remember who Thomas was before this, too.
Earlier in John, when Jesus decides to go back toward danger, it's Thomas who tells the others, "Let us also go, that we may die with him." The nickname doubting Thomas isn't in the Bible.
Some readers would rather say honest Thomas, or brave Thomas.
Catholics also keep this Sunday as Divine Mercy Sunday, a day centered on God's mercy, and some hear the two fitting together: a wounded Christ, offering peace, to a friend who couldn't yet believe.

how: In a number of churches, John 20's story of Thomas is read on the Sunday after Easter; the Orthodox call it Thomas Sunday, and Catholics also keep it as Divine Mercy Sunday.

games.q: Thomas, line by line — tap the pairs.

s: John says Thomas put his finger in the wounds
Jesus offers, but the text goes straight to Thomas saying "my Lord and my God."
the phrase doubting Thomas comes from the Bible
it's a later nickname. John's Thomas also says "let us also go, that we may die with him."
Jesus answers Thomas's terms almost word for word
finger, hands, side: what Thomas asked for is what he's offered.

games.q: you're Thomas. your friends say they've seen Jesus alive, and you weren't there. what do you say?
o: "unless I see the nails and touch his side, I will not believe."
games.why: Thomas names his terms. eight days later Jesus meets them, and Thomas says "my Lord and my God."

practice: Let one honest question come up, about faith or about anything you're asked to trust, and don't argue it down or polish it. Say it to yourself plainly, the way Thomas did, with your terms: this is what it would take.
If you pray, bring that doubt to God just as it is; if you don't, hold the question with a bit of respect, as a sign you're paying attention.

wordCard.voice: Thomas Sunday. The Sunday after Easter, remembering the disciple who said what it would take to believe, and then said, my Lord and my God.

orig.note: Greek: twin. John calls him Thomas, called Didymus.
